Q: Unit testing - Find code coverage for conditions in mysql queries A:

You have answered your own question while asking "Query has to execute at leaset 3 times with different vakues [sic] of a_col to complete the coverage. How to ensure that coverage."

This is more of a unit test question than code coverage question. Any code coverage tool will consider the statement as being fully covered if the statement is called just once. Therefore your unit tests would need to account for each predicate evaluation that would need to be checked and so you will need to write at least three different tests, or, one test which includes a result set where a_col has all the required different values you wish to check for. Which is best is up to yourself.

Q: x axis label cropped on saved image A:

Very simple 1 line solution

There is a very simple solution to this: Add bbox_inches='tight' as an argument to savefig.

plt.savefig('example.png', bbox_inches='tight')

Q: Is cache coherency only an issue when storing and not when loading? A:

As very well mentioned in the other answer, the (L3, L2, L1) caches are coherent, but the (small) store buffers (also known as write buffers) (associated with each SMT/Hyperthreading Hardware Threading Unit of each Core) are not coherent, and special instructions (applied to properly aligned scalar objects in memory) need to be applied when ordering (or, more generally, synchronization) is needed.

Synchronization = Indivisibility + Ordering + Other Guarantees.

For the x86/x64 Architecture, I think we can find the ordering guarantees in the "Intel 64 Architecture Memory Ordering White Paper" (approx. 2007). This short document has since been merged in the Software Developer Manuals for Intel, but it can still be found on the Internet.

(AMD might have similar documents.)

For the x86, I think that only the std::memory_order_seq_cst atomic store needs a special instruction (xchg) or sequence of instructions (mov + mfence) and that the std::memory_order_release atomic store can be implemented with a normal instruction (mov).

Generally it is best to use the sequence agreed upon with other pieces of code which we link against, e.g. if all compilers use the xchg instruction for the std::memory_order_seq_cst atomic store, we should not use the alternative sequence (mov + mfence) in our machine code.

Another possibility is to implement the std::memory_order_seq_cst atomic stores with simple mov and [edit -- I had initially specified a wrong sequence -- please see the link in Peter Cordes' comment -- and I thank him !!] [later edit: Now I see that mov + mfence [was in fact a viable implementation](https://www.decadent.org.uk/pipermail/cpp-threads/2008-December/001933.html), so maybe not wrong after all !!] implement std::memory_order_seq_cst atomic loads as a sequence which includes the fencing, but in addition to the linking problem, this would incur penalty on atomic loads, whereas currently atomic loads incur no penalty as compared to normal loads, and loads are more numerous than stores => this would be an even worse choice.
